query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Sn (on the order of a few atomic percent) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures by forming a Sn-enriched protective oxide scale without substantially compromising its intrinsic room‐ and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with a single-phase BCC microstructure exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying modification achieved by adding a few atomic percent of Sn in the melt (either by substitution or slight supplementation) during casting.
generation.conditions: Air exposure at approximately 800 °C for a duration up to 5 hours; mechanical performance to be maintained during subsequent high-temperature loading (e.g., at strain rates from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹).
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent Sn-containing oxide (likely SnO or SnO₂) that forms on the alloy surface during high temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: The Sn addition preferentially oxidizes to form a thin, stable oxide scale that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy, thereby mitigating oxygen-induced embrittlement (pesting) while leaving the BCC structure and bulk mechanical properties largely unaffected.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Sn-modified alloy will display reduced oxidation (lower weight gain and thinner oxide scale) and maintain comparable tensile ductility at room temperature and high-temperature yield strength under the specified conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is known to exhibit inadequate oxygen resistance at high temperatures despite its acceptable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: Temperature at or near 800 °C, exposure time around 5 hours in air, and mechanical loading conditions similar to the reported strain rates (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹); ensuring that the Sn addition does not alter phase stability or significantly reduce ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Sn concentration and its effect on phase stability and ductility require careful optimization. There is also uncertainty about how the Sn-modified oxide scale will interact with the high-temperature deformation mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and one with a minor addition (e.g., 3 at.%) of Sn. Process both via identical casting and heat-treatment procedures to obtain a similar single-phase BCC microstructure. Expose both sample sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, conduct detailed oxide scale characterization (using SEM, TEM, and weight gain measurements) and perform tensile tests at room temperature and at high temperatures (near 1000 °C) at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar oxide scale thickness or weight gain) or if its mechanical properties (ductility or high-temperature strength) are degraded compared to the untreated alloy under the same conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,].
